clue.text: Old policeman's inclination to take attractive person hugging gnarled tree, right?

parts.note: a bow is an inclination of the head or body

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap arms around, so one piece wraps around the others

parts.note: a stunner is a very attractive person

indicators.note: something gnarled is twisted and knotted, so these letters are twisted out of order

parts.note: taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A tree-hugging lawman takes a fancy to a beautiful companion beside a twisted old trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The attractive person wraps around the jumbled tree and the R. The Bow Street Runners were London's first professional police force, founded in the eighteenth century at Bow Street magistrates' court.
explanation.definitionFit: The Runners were an early London constabulary, so one member is a historical example of an old-time officer.

clue.text: American writer a good deal tense about chapter

indicators.note: 'about' here means surrounding, so the outer letters go round the inner one

parts.note: a lot means a good deal
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
C is a standard abbreviation for chapter

explanation.surface: A critic notes that an American author spends a great deal of strained effort on one chapter.
explanation.walkthrough: A LOT and T sit side by side and together go round C, giving AL-C-OT-T.
explanation.definitionFit: Louisa May Alcott, who wrote Little Women, is a famous nineteenth-century novelist from Massachusetts.

clue.text: Better periods after skipping British tour

indicators.note: to skip something is to leave it out, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: bouts are periods of activity
B is the abbreviation for British
a trip is a tour or journey

explanation.surface: Things improved for a traveller once the British leg of the tour was skipped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' is a verb here, not an adjective, and 'after' just means the tour follows the shortened periods.
explanation.definitionFit: To better a rival is to surpass or exceed them, which is exactly what outstripping means.

clue.text: Good friends to dine — ten, possibly? Planning for the best

parts.note: to be well in with someone is to be on good friendly terms

indicators.note: 'possibly' says these letters are only one possible arrangement, so rearrange them

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A hopeful host plans a dinner for ten close friends, hoping it all goes well.
explanation.walkthrough: WELL IN is the British phrase for being on friendly terms with someone; the other nine letters are a jumble of 'to dine ten'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone well-intentioned means well and has good aims, hoping for a good outcome even if things go wrong.

clue.text: American science probing nothing — it's just a front

indicators.note: a probe pushes inside something, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: FA, short for 'sweet FA', is British slang for nothing at all
A is the abbreviation for American
SCI is the short form of science

explanation.surface: A cynic dismisses American science as hollow: it is all show, a mere front.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet FA is a mild British euphemism for 'nothing at all'; the science goes inside it, splitting it into F and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A fascia is the board over a shopfront bearing its name, or a car's dashboard panel: a facing surface.

clue.text: Pen German song about Society in elaborate fashion?

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase defining an adjective

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs

indicators.note: 'about' here means surrounding, so one piece is placed around another

parts.note: a Lied is a German art song
S is the abbreviation for Society

explanation.surface: Someone writes a German song about high society in a showy, ornate manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like a verb for writing; it is the noun, an animal enclosure. LIED wraps round S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something stylised is rendered in a conventional, non-naturalistic manner, with artful flourishes rather than realism.

clue.text: Mountaineer's statement wildly cheers beauties seen around heart of mountains

indicators.note: acting wildly means behaving without order, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only its middle letter is kept

parts.note: the central letter of the nine-letter word

explanation.surface: A climber cheers wildly at the beautiful peaks all around.
explanation.walkthrough: The fourteen letters of 'cheers beauties' plus the T from the middle of 'mountains' are jumbled together.
explanation.definitionFit: George Mallory famously gave this reply when asked why he wanted to climb Everest, making it a celebrated climber's quotation.

clue.text: French painter indicated by easel, colour and tutu, possibly

indicators.note: 'possibly' marks these letters as one possible form of something else, so rearrange them

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An easel, paints and a ballet dancer's tutu suggest which French artist is meant.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits nicely: he painted dancers of Montmartre, so a tutu feels like a genuine hint, but it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec was a nineteenth-century artist famed for posters and scenes of Parisian nightlife.

clue.text: Good women avoiding industrial action in European city

indicators.note: to avoid something is to keep away from it, so those letters are left out

parts.note: a go-slow is a form of industrial action where workers deliberately slow down
W is the abbreviation for women
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Virtuous women steer clear of a strike while visiting a continental city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good women' reads like a description of people; it is two abbreviations to be removed from GO-SLOW.
explanation.definitionFit: Oslo is the capital of Norway, a Scandinavian country in northern Europe.

clue.text: Wit and wine — a feature of the table?

parts.note: salt, as in 'Attic salt', means sharp wit
a cellar is a stock of wine

explanation.surface: Clever conversation and good wine are what make a dinner party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wit and wine' sound like table talk and drink, but each word is replaced by a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A salt cellar is the small dish or shaker holding salt, a standard item set out on a dining table.

clue.text: Monks initially ready to tuck into a lot of tea subsequently

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter goes

parts.note: brew is tea, cut short by one letter

indicators.note: to tuck into something is to go inside it, so one letter is placed within another word

parts.note: then means subsequently or afterwards

indicators.note: 'initially' points to the start, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Monks first get ready, then settle down to a big pot of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: A brew is British slang for a pot or cup of tea, here missing its last letter; the R is tucked into the word for subsequently.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of a religious order address each other as brothers, and brethren is the old plural used for such fellow members.

clue.text: A lot of aid heading for Italy or place there …

indicators.note: a lot of something falls short of all of it, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: assist means aid, with its last letter removed

indicators.note: a heading sits at the top, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of the country

explanation.surface: Much of the relief money is going to Italy, or to one particular town there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there' refers back to Italy, so the definition is an Italian place. The ellipsis leads into the next clue, which continues the thought.
explanation.definitionFit: Assisi is a hill town in Umbria, central Italy, famous as the birthplace of Saint Francis.

clue.text: … with another apparently discouraging tourists?

parts.note: continuing from the previous clue: another Italian place, in a famous saying about it
taken literally, a saying ordering visitors to perish sounds like a dreadful advertisement for travel

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb means a city is so beautiful that nothing after it could compare; read literally it sounds like a threat to visitors. 'Another' is a second Italian place after Assisi.
explanation.definitionFit: This old proverb praises the Bay of Naples as the finest sight in life, though literally it tells visitors to perish.

clue.text: Aristo with unusual male name?

parts.note: a nob is British slang for a wealthy upper-class person

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so these letters come out of their usual order

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: An aristocrat bears some odd, distinctive man's name, as such people often do.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: a titled man often carries an unusual name.
explanation.definitionFit: A titled peer of the realm is an aristocrat, and lords often have uncommon double-barrelled family names.

clue.text: Story and a remark about European recording

indicators.note: 'about' here means around, so one word encloses the others

parts.note: taken as written
a note is a brief written remark
E is the abbreviation for European
a CD, compact disc, is a recording

explanation.surface: A tale accompanied by a comment on a European album.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recording' is easy to read as an activity, but it stands for a compact disc, which joins E inside the remark.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a short amusing or interesting account of a real incident, a kind of tale.

clue.text: Productive moral tale, but lacking power

indicators.note: to lack something is to be without it, so a letter goes missing

parts.note: a parable is a story told to teach a moral
P is the abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: A fable that teaches a useful lesson yet has no real force behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: PARABLE loses its P.
explanation.definitionFit: Arable land is fertile soil suitable for growing crops, so it yields harvests and is fruitful.

clue.text: Expression of hesitation over second town guide, dropping old fake

indicators.note: to drop something is to let it go, so a letter is lost

parts.note: er is the sound people make when hesitating
S is the abbreviation for second
an A to Z is a street map book for a British town, best known for London
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone dithers over a town map before rejecting it as a counterfeit.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' means placed above, so ER sits on top. A to Z is the brand of street atlas found in every British car.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz, borrowed from German, describes an inferior substitute or imitation, so it means artificial or bogus.

clue.text: Thinker is probing the bit left over

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a probe goes inside something, so one piece is pushed into another

parts.note: an ort is a scrap of food left over after a meal
taken as written

explanation.surface: A philosopher pokes around in the leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: An ort is an old word for a scrap left after a meal, known today mainly from crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorist develops abstract ideas and explanations, so is someone whose work is reasoning and ideas.

clue.text: Discount Republican replacing Democrat in discussion

indicators.note: to replace is to take another's place, so one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: a debate is a formal discussion
R is the abbreviation for Republican
D is the abbreviation for Democrat

explanation.surface: A US political argument where one party's member ousts the other's, and one side is dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discount' looks like a verb meaning dismiss; it is the noun. The D of DEBATE becomes R.
explanation.definitionFit: A rebate is a partial refund or reduction on an amount paid, which is a kind of price cut.

clue.text: Roger droned to us, unfortunately

indicators.note: something that turned out unfortunately went wrong, so these letters have gone awry

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Roger bored his listeners with a monotonous speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roger' poses as a man's name; it is the radio word for a message received.
explanation.definitionFit: In radio procedure, saying 'roger' confirms a message has been received and its meaning grasped.

clue.text: Scientist suspending oxygen and hydrogen in bromine

indicators.note: a substance suspended in a liquid sits within it, so these letters sit inside another pair

parts.note: Br is the chemical symbol for bromine, from the periodic table
H is the chemical symbol for hydrogen
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A chemist holds oxygen and hydrogen suspended in bromine during an experiment.
explanation.walkthrough: All three chemical symbols suit the laboratory surface; O and H go inside BR.
explanation.definitionFit: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who won the Nobel Prize for his model of atomic structure.

clue.text: Leave advisor to cross street in front of English shop

parts.note: to depart is to leave

indicators.note: to have something cross you is to have it pass through your middle, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: a mentor is a trusted advisor
ST is the abbreviation for street
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A counsellor suggests going out across the road to a shop selling English goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' looks like a noun for time off; it is the verb. The street abbreviation sits inside the advisor, then English follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A department store is a large retail building divided into sections selling many kinds of goods.
